External links for this lesson. All checked to load from a plain request as of the date this
page was written. (Note: eCFR's own site — ecfr.gov — blocks automated/proxied traffic with a
bot check in this repo's build environment, even though a human browser reaches it fine; the
regulation text quoted in this lesson comes from eCFR's public Versioner API instead, and the
links below use verified-loading mirrors of the same official text.)

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 606.165, current text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/606.165)**
  — the distribution and receipt record requirements this lesson quotes to mark the exact point
  a unit crosses from Lakeshore's system of record into a hospital's.

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 606.170, current text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/606.170)**
  — the adverse reaction file and fatality reporting requirements this lesson builds its
  transfusion-reaction section around, including the forwarding obligation that keeps Lakeshore
  in the loop after a reaction is traced to the product.

- **[Cornell LII: 21 CFR 600.15, current text](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/600.15)**
  — the full shipping-temperature table this lesson excerpts, including the row for Red Blood
  Cells and every other blood product on the list; also shows the vaccine products this lesson
  didn't quote, since the section covers all of Part 600's biologics, not just blood.

- **[GovInfo: Code of Federal Regulations](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/collection/cfr)** — the
  U.S. Government Publishing Office's official, legally authoritative annual CFR archive. Use
  this for the official, dated, legally citable version of a specific year's text — for example,
  to confirm exactly what 606.170 said on the date of a past reaction investigation.

- **[Blood Transfusions - Medical-Surgical (Med-Surg) - Cardiovascular
  System](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P6sfE4T9FvM)** (Level Up RN, from oEmbed
  `author_name`) — the video embedded in this lesson. Nursing-education content on transfusion
  reactions: the signs, symptoms, and immediate bedside response (stopping the transfusion) that
  this module's regulatory chain picks up from after the fact. Not about Lakeshore, BECS, or any
  CFR citation in this lesson — it's the clinical moment the 606.170(a) investigation requirement
  responds to. Verified embeddable via YouTube oEmbed on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[AABB: Hemovigilance](https://www.aabb.org/blood-biotherapies/blood/transfusion-medicine/hemovigilance)**
  (redirects from `aabb.org/news-resources/resources/hemovigilance`, confirmed landing page) —
  AABB's own page on hemovigilance as a practice: tracking and reporting adverse events tied to
  blood products and transfusions, the general framework this lesson's ITSM bridge maps onto
  "incident reporting with an external regulator on the distribution list." Use this for the
  standards-tier view of hemovigilance that sits alongside — not instead of — 606.170's
  regulatory requirement. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 301 → 200 on the
  redirected URL).

- **[CDC NHSN: Biovigilance Component — Hemovigilance
  Module](https://www.cdc.gov/nhsn/biovigilance/index.html)** — the U.S. National Healthcare
  Safety Network's own hemovigilance surveillance program, run by CDC rather than FDA: hospitals
  and blood centers that participate report transfusion-related adverse events into this system
  as a public-health surveillance layer that exists alongside, not instead of, the 606.170
  reporting obligations this lesson covers. Useful for seeing hemovigilance as a field with its
  own national infrastructure, not just a single regulation. **Verification note:** this page
  returned HTTP 200 to a `HEAD` request but HTTP 403 to a `GET` on independent re-check — the
  same Akamai/CDC automated-traffic bot check this curriculum has already seen block eCFR and
  FDA pages from this build environment while a human browser reaches them fine. Treat this the
  same way: likely reachable in a real browser, not independently confirmed with a full page
  fetch this session.

- **[TechTarget: What is a laboratory information system
  (LIS)?](https://www.techtarget.com/searchhealthit/definition/laboratory-information-system)** —
  a vendor-neutral healthcare-IT explainer of what an LIS actually does and how it differs from a
  hospital's broader EHR/HIS systems — the general version of the LIS/HIS distinction this
  lesson draws specifically for Riverside's systems. Read this for the industry-standard
  vocabulary; the lesson's own text is what ties it to 606.165's handoff. Verified loading via
  `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

## Keep learning

Not official sources — good places to learn more about transfusion reactions and what hemovigilance catches.

- **[069CE: Preventing TRALI with Beth Shaz](https://www.bbguy.org/2019/05/22/069/)** (Blood Bank Guy podcast) — how a serious reaction (transfusion-related acute lung injury) is investigated back to the donor and product, and how prevention changed inventory practice. Shows why traceability data matters. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[066: IgA Deficiency and Anaphylactic Reactions with Jerry Sandler](https://www.bbguy.org/2019/04/10/066/)** (Blood Bank Guy podcast) — a second reaction case study; useful for seeing what a hospital reports back to the supplier and what that implies for your records. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
- **[BBGuy Essentials 003: septic transfusion reactions with Dr. Anne Eder (transcript, PDF)](https://www.bbguy.org/pdf/BBGE_003_Anne_Eder_Transcript.pdf)** (Blood Bank Guy podcast) — a lookback and recall example: a contaminated platelet unit and what follows. Details predate later FDA guidance. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200; PDF, no HTML title).
